## Planning Range for Lantana Control Duration at Elephants by the Lake

### Site identification

"Elephants by the Lake" almost certainly refers to the Kabini backwaters area on the southeastern boundary of Nagarhole National Park, Karnataka -- the iconic site where elephant super-herds congregate at the reservoir during the dry season. This places it squarely in the **Western Ghats moist-dry deciduous transition zone**, with annual rainfall of roughly 800-1200 mm, surrounded by extensive Lantana-invaded forest in both Nagarhole and adjacent Bandipur Tiger Reserve (67% Lantana cover in Bandipur alone).

### Method: evidence-to-planning-range derivation

I extracted quantitative timelines from five published sources, then adjusted for site-specific factors at Kabini.

**Source data used:**

| Source | Site | Removal method | Key finding |
|---|---|---|---|
| Prasad, Ratnam & Sankaran (2018), *Biol. Invasions* 20:3399-3407 | Southern Indian deciduous forests (Bandipur/BRT area) | Uprooting vs. cutting | Uprooting + post-monsoon weeding minimised re-invasion; cutting alone led to rapid coppicing. Wetter sites had higher re-invasion from seed & rootstock but better native recovery. |
| Ramaswami, Prasad, Westcott, Subuddhi & Sukumar (2014), *Indian Forester* 140(2):129-136 | Rajaji NP, Uttarakhand | Standard mechanical removal (1 or 2 years) | "Rapid recolonisation" from seed dispersal, soil seed bank, and vegetative regrowth even after 2 consecutive years of management. |
| Junglescapes / CEPF-ATREE (2013-2015), Final project report, Bandipur TR | Bandipur Tiger Reserve (Lokkere RF) | Cut Root-Stock (CRS) method | ~15% re-emergence in Year 2, ~5% in Year 3. 98% eradication success in moderate-density areas, 80% in high-density. Model sustained >6 years with follow-up. |
| Sundaram, Prasad & Hiremath (2018), *Indian Forester* 144(6):545-552 | BRT Tiger Reserve, Western Ghats | Cutting+burning vs. uprooting | "No Lantana removal is likely to be effective without post-removal monitoring and weeding." |
| Vivian-Smith & Panetta (2009), *Invasive Plant Sci. & Management* 2(2):141-150 | Queensland, Australia (globally applicable seed bank data) | Seed burial experiment | Seed bank persistence modeled at 3 yr (irrigated) to 11 yr (buried, natural rainfall). Seeds remain germinable at 25-27% after 2-3 years. |

**Seed bank viability** is the hard constraint. Multiple reviews cite 2-5 years (Wijayabandara et al. 2011, compiled in Bhagwat et al. 2012 and others). Vivian-Smith & Panetta (2009) modeled up to 11 years for deeply buried seeds under natural rainfall. Indian operational programs (CAMPA 2022 proposal) explicitly state "lantana seeds have viability of more than one year and keep on germinating," with Bandipur protocols budgeting follow-up weeding through Year 5.

### Derivation of the planning range

**Scenario A -- One-time removal, no follow-up (slash/burn or single uprooting):**
- Coppicing from rootstock begins within the first post-monsoon season (3-6 months).
- Seed bank germination restores ground cover within 1-2 monsoons.
- Functional Lantana canopy re-established: **1-2 years**.
- Source: Ramaswami et al. (2014); Prasad et al. (2018); Sundaram et al. (2018).

**Scenario B -- Best-practice removal (CRS or full uprooting) with 2-3 years of annual follow-up weeding:**
- Year 1: initial clearance.
- Year 2: ~15% re-emergence, weeded.
- Year 3: ~5% re-emergence, weeded.
- If follow-up stops after Year 3, residual seed bank (still 5-20% viable) plus bird-dispersed propagule pressure from surrounding invaded forest means reinvasion begins within 1-3 further years.
- Effective control duration from initial clearance: **3-5 years**.
- Source: Junglescapes/CEPF-ATREE Bandipur data; Prasad et al. (2018).

**Scenario C -- Best-practice removal with 5+ years of follow-up AND active native restoration (grass/bamboo seeding, canopy establishment):**
- This is the Bandipur/Junglescapes model that has demonstrated sustained control over 6+ years and ~1,500 ha.
- Native grass and bamboo establish competitive canopy closure that suppresses new Lantana recruits.
- If native canopy closes successfully, the site can become self-sustaining against re-invasion.
- Effective control duration: **5-8+ years**, potentially indefinite if native community establishes.
- Source: Junglescapes sustained model (>6 years documented); CAMPA 2022 protocol (5-year follow-up budget); Vivian-Smith & Panetta (2009) seed bank exhaustion model.

### Site-specific adjustments for Kabini / Nagarhole

Three factors work against control longevity here:

1. **High propagule pressure.** Kabini is embedded within one of the most Lantana-invaded landscapes in the Western Ghats. Bird-mediated seed rain from surrounding forest will be continuous and heavy.
2. **Intermediate-to-high rainfall.** Prasad et al. (2018) showed that wetter sites have greater re-invasion from seed and rootstock, requiring more effort.
3. **Elephant disturbance.** The defining feature of this site -- large elephant herds -- creates soil disturbance and canopy gaps that favor Lantana germination (high light + soil temperature triggers).

One factor works in favor: the seasonal flooding/drawdown cycle at the reservoir margin may periodically suppress Lantana in the littoral zone.

### Planning range recommendation

| Scenario | Expected control duration | Budget assumption |
|---|---|---|
| **One-time clearance, no follow-up** | **1-2 years** | Waste of money in this landscape |
| **CRS + 3 years annual weeding** | **3-5 years** from first clearance | Minimum viable program |
| **CRS + 5 years weeding + native restoration** | **5-8 years**, potentially self-sustaining | Recommended program |

**For planning purposes, use 3-5 years as your central range**, meaning: budget for at least 3 annual follow-up treatments after initial clearance, and expect to need a maintenance pass every 2-3 years thereafter unless native canopy closure is achieved. If you do only a single clearance, plan for full re-invasion within 2 monsoon seasons.

### Caveats and checkable assumptions

1. I assumed "Elephants by the Lake" = Kabini/Nagarhole. If it is a different site, the rainfall and propagule-pressure adjustments change.
2. The Junglescapes 15%/5% re-emergence figures are from moderate-density CRS removal. High-density areas showed only 80% initial success, meaning re-emergence would be worse.
3. No published study from this exact site reports Lantana control duration. The planning range is extrapolated from Bandipur (adjacent, same forest type, same rainfall zone), BRT (same Western Ghats landscape, ~100 km south), and Rajaji NP (different rainfall zone but same species ecology).
4. Seed bank viability of 2-5 years (reviews) to 11 years (experimental extreme) is the hard lower bound on follow-up duration. The 3-year minimum I recommend is aggressive; 5 years is safer.

- Ramaswami G, Prasad S, Westcott D, Subuddhi SP, Sukumar R (2014) Addressing the management of a long-established invasive shrub: the case of *Lantana camara* in Indian forests. *Indian Forester* 140(2):129-136.
- Sundaram B, Prasad A, Hiremath AJ (2018) Restoring *Lantana camara* invaded tropical deciduous forest. *Indian Forester* 144(6):545-552.
- Junglescapes Charitable Trust (2014) CEPF-ATREE Final Project Report: Integrated project for lantana management, Lokkere RF, Bandipur. Available at indiabiodiversity.org.
- Vivian-Smith G, Panetta FD (2009) Lantana (*Lantana camara*) seed bank dynamics: seedling emergence and seed survival. *Invasive Plant Science and Management* 2(2):141-150.
- CAMPA (2022) Collaborative revised project proposal for lantana management. National CAMPA Advisory Council, India.
- Ramaswami G, Sukumar R (2013) Long-term environmental correlates of invasion by *Lantana camara* in a seasonally dry tropical forest. *PLoS ONE* 8:e76995.

Lantana camara is highly persistent in the Western Ghats, and attempts at eradication often result in rapid regrowth from rootstocks and the soil seed bank [1][2][3][4]. Effective long-term control requires more than one-time removal; it necessitates uprooting rather than cutting, as cutting leads to aggressive coppicing [1][2][5]. <content>The success of invasive species eradication depends on a variety of factors, including those that initially facilitated the invasion, as well as removal and post-removal protocols. Two factors that appear to influence invasion by, and eradication of, the Neotropical shrub Lantana camara (L.), in southern Indian deciduous forests, are rainfall and removal method. We conducted an experiment to clarify how rainfall (high vs. low) and removal method (cutting vs. uprooting Lantana) influence re-invasion by Lantana, and native plant recovery. Rainfall influenced both eradication effort and outcomes—drier forest had lower starting levels of invader biomass, requiring less initial eradication effort, as well as lower subsequent Lantana re-invasion (from seed and rootstock) whereas wetter forest typically had greater starting levels of invader biomass, requiring considerably greater initial eradication effort, and greater Lantana re-invasion. However, wetter forest also showed greater native tree and forb recovery. Therefore, the availability of funds, local environmental gradients, and restoration priorities should inform the selection of restoration sites. With regard to removal method, uprooting combined with weeding of germinating Lantana, particularly after the rainy season, minimized overall re-invasion. Therefore, uprooting, followed by regular weeding of germinating Lantana and secondary invaders, is crucial to long-term Lantana eradication success.

<content>The success of invasive species eradication depends on a variety of factors, including those that initially facilitated the invasion, as well as removal and post-removal protocols. Two factors that appear to influence invasion by, and eradication of, the Neotropical shrub Lantana camara (L.), in southern Indian deciduous forests, are rainfall and removal method. We conducted an experiment to clarify how rainfall (high vs. low) and removal method (cutting vs. uprooting Lantana) influence re-invasion by Lantana, and native plant recovery. However, wetter forest also showed greater native tree and forb recovery. Therefore, the availability of funds, local environmental gradients, and restoration priorities should inform the selection of restoration sites. With regard to removal method, uprooting combined with weeding of germinating Lantana, particularly after the rainy season, minimized overall re-invasion. ---

## Planning Range for Lantana Control Duration at Elephants by the Lake

### Site identification

"Elephants by the Lake" almost certainly refers to the Kabini backwaters area on the southeastern boundary of Nagarhole National Park, Karnataka -- the iconic site where elephant super-herds congregate at the reservoir during the dry season. This places it squarely in the **Western Ghats moist-dry deciduous transition zone**, with annual rainfall of roughly 800-1200 mm, surrounded by extensive Lantana-invaded forest in both Nagarhole and adjacent Bandipur Tiger Reserve (67% Lantana cover in Bandipur alone).

### Method: evidence-to-planning-range derivation

I extracted quantitative timelines from five published sources, then adjusted for site-specific factors at Kabini.

**Source data used:**

| Source | Site | Removal method | Key finding |
|---|---|---|---|
| Prasad, Ratnam & Sankaran (2018), *Biol. Invasions* 20:3399-3407 | Southern Indian deciduous forests (Bandipur/BRT area) | Uprooting vs. cutting | Uprooting + post-monsoon weeding minimised re-invasion; cutting alone led to rapid coppicing. Wetter sites had higher re-invasion from seed & rootstock but better native recovery. |
| Ramaswami, Prasad, Westcott, Subuddhi & Sukumar (2014), *Indian Forester* 140(2):129-136 | Rajaji NP, Uttarakhand | Standard mechanical removal (1 or 2 years) | "Rapid recolonisation" from seed dispersal, soil seed bank, and vegetative regrowth even after 2 consecutive years of management. |
| Junglescapes / CEPF-ATREE (2013-2015), Final project report, Bandipur TR | Bandipur Tiger Reserve (Lokkere RF) | Cut Root-Stock (CRS) method | ~15% re-emergence in Year 2, ~5% in Year 3. 98% eradication success in moderate-density areas, 80% in high-density. Model sustained >6 years with follow-up. |
| Sundaram, Prasad & Hiremath (2018), *Indian Forester* 144(6):545-552 | BRT Tiger Reserve, Western Ghats | Cutting+burning vs. uprooting | "No Lantana removal is likely to be effective without post-removal monitoring and weeding." |
| Vivian-Smith & Panetta (2009), *Invasive Plant Sci. & Management* 2(2):141-150 | Queensland, Australia (globally applicable seed bank data) | Seed burial experiment | Seed bank persistence modeled at 3 yr (irrigated) to 11 yr (buried, natural rainfall). Seeds remain germinable at 25-27% after 2-3 years. |

**Seed bank viability** is the hard constraint. Multiple reviews cite 2-5 years (Wijayabandara et al. 2011, compiled in Bhagwat et al. 2012 and others). Vivian-Smith & Panetta (2009) modeled up to 11 years for deeply buried seeds under natural rainfall. Indian operational programs (CAMPA 2022 proposal) explicitly state "lantana seeds have viability of more than one year and keep on germinating," with Bandipur protocols budgeting follow-up weeding through Year 5.

### Derivation of the planning range

**Scenario A -- One-time removal, no follow-up (slash/burn or single uprooting):**
- Coppicing from rootstock begins within the first post-monsoon season (3-6 months).
- Seed bank germination restores ground cover within 1-2 monsoons.
- Functional Lantana canopy re-established: **1-2 years**.
- Source: Ramaswami et al. (2014); Prasad et al. (2018); Sundaram et al. (2018).

**Scenario B -- Best-practice removal (CRS or full uprooting) with 2-3 years of annual follow-up weeding:**
- Year 1: initial clearance.
- Year 2: ~15% re-emergence, weeded.
- Year 3: ~5% re-emergence, weeded.
- If follow-up stops after Year 3, residual seed bank (still 5-20% viable) plus bird-dispersed propagule pressure from surrounding invaded forest means reinvasion begins within 1-3 further years.
- Effective control duration from initial clearance: **3-5 years**.
- Source: Junglescapes/CEPF-ATREE Bandipur data; Prasad et al. (2018).

**Scenario C -- Best-practice removal with 5+ years of follow-up AND active native restoration (grass/bamboo seeding, canopy establishment):**
- This is the Bandipur/Junglescapes model that has demonstrated sustained control over 6+ years and ~1,500 ha.
- Native grass and bamboo establish competitive canopy closure that suppresses new Lantana recruits.
- If native canopy closes successfully, the site can become self-sustaining against re-invasion.
- Effective control duration: **5-8+ years**, potentially indefinite if native community establishes.
- Source: Junglescapes sustained model (>6 years documented); CAMPA 2022 protocol (5-year follow-up budget); Vivian-Smith & Panetta (2009) seed bank exhaustion model.

### Site-specific adjustments for Kabini / Nagarhole

Three factors work against control longevity here:

1. **High propagule pressure.** Kabini is embedded within one of the most Lantana-invaded landscapes in the Western Ghats. Bird-mediated seed rain from surrounding forest will be continuous and heavy.
2. **Intermediate-to-high rainfall.** Prasad et al. (2018) showed that wetter sites have greater re-invasion from seed and rootstock, requiring more effort.
3. **Elephant disturbance.** The defining feature of this site -- large elephant herds -- creates soil disturbance and canopy gaps that favor Lantana germination (high light + soil temperature triggers).

One factor works in favor: the seasonal flooding/drawdown cycle at the reservoir margin may periodically suppress Lantana in the littoral zone.

### Planning range recommendation

| Scenario | Expected control duration | Budget assumption |
|---|---|---|
| **One-time clearance, no follow-up** | **1-2 years** | Waste of money in this landscape |
| **CRS + 3 years annual weeding** | **3-5 years** from first clearance | Minimum viable program |
| **CRS + 5 years weeding + native restoration** | **5-8 years**, potentially self-sustaining | Recommended program |

**For planning purposes, use 3-5 years as your central range**, meaning: budget for at least 3 annual follow-up treatments after initial clearance, and expect to need a maintenance pass every 2-3 years thereafter unless native canopy closure is achieved. If you do only a single clearance, plan for full re-invasion within 2 monsoon seasons.

### Caveats and checkable assumptions

1. I assumed "Elephants by the Lake" = Kabini/Nagarhole. If it is a different site, the rainfall and propagule-pressure adjustments change.
2. The Junglescapes 15%/5% re-emergence figures are from moderate-density CRS removal. High-density areas showed only 80% initial success, meaning re-emergence would be worse.
3. No published study from this exact site reports Lantana control duration. The planning range is extrapolated from Bandipur (adjacent, same forest type, same rainfall zone), BRT (same Western Ghats landscape, ~100 km south), and Rajaji NP (different rainfall zone but same species ecology).
4. Seed bank viability of 2-5 years (reviews) to 11 years (experimental extreme) is the hard lower bound on follow-up duration. The 3-year minimum I recommend is aggressive; 5 years is safer.

### Key citations

- Prasad A, Ratnam J, Sankaran M (2018) Rainfall and removal method influence eradication success for *Lantana camara*. *Biological Invasions* 20:3399-3407.
- Ramaswami G, Prasad S, Westcott D, Subuddhi SP, Sukumar R (2014) Addressing the management of a long-established invasive shrub: the case of *Lantana camara* in Indian forests. *Indian Forester* 140(2):129-136.
- Sundaram B, Prasad A, Hiremath AJ (2018) Restoring *Lantana camara* invaded tropical deciduous forest. *Indian Forester* 144(6):545-552.
- Junglescapes Charitable Trust (2014) CEPF-ATREE Final Project Report: Integrated project for lantana management, Lokkere RF, Bandipur. Available at indiabiodiversity.org.
- Vivian-Smith G, Panetta FD (2009) Lantana (*Lantana camara*) seed bank dynamics: seedling emergence and seed survival. *Invasive Plant Science and Management* 2(2):141-150.
- CAMPA (2022) Collaborative revised project proposal for lantana management. National CAMPA Advisory Council, India.
- Ramaswami G, Sukumar R (2013) Long-term environmental correlates of invasion by *Lantana camara* in a seasonally dry tropical forest. *PLoS ONE* 8:e76995.
